### **Encoded and non-genetic protein variants** 

### **expand human functional proteome** 

3 4 Vyacheslav Tretyachenko<sup>1</sup> #, Tehila Leiman<sup>1</sup> , David Morgenstern<sup>2</sup> , Yishai Levin<sup>2</sup> , Omer Asraf<sup>1</sup> , Orna 5 Dahan<sup>1</sup> , Dvir Dahary<sup>1</sup> , Yitzhak Pilpel<sup>1</sup> # 6 1Department of Molecular Genetics, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, 76100, Israel 7 2Nancy and Stephen Grand Israel National Center for Personalized Medicine G-INCPM, Weizmann 8 Institute of Science, 760001 Rehovot, Israel 9 #corresponding authors at the above address: tretyacv@gmail.com; pilpel@weizmann.ac.il 10 11 **Each stage of the Central Dogma contributes to proteome diversity through mechanisms** 12 **such as heterozygosity, somatic mutations, transcriptional errors, and translational** 13 **errors. As a result, a diverse array of protein variants can coexist within a single** 14 **proteome, such as that of humans. However, until now, methods to detect, quantify, and** 15 **evaluate the functional consequences of these variants have been lacking. Here we** 16 **examined a large-scale proteogenomic dataset from 29 healthy human tissues and** 17 **uncovered 13,910 confidently localized variants representing 7,215 unique single amino** 18 **acid substitutions co-existing alongside their corresponding reference proteoforms**<sup>1</sup> **.We** 19 **found that the abundance of both genetic (SNP’s, somatic mutations) and mistranslated** 20 **protein variants mirrors their allele frequencies in the human population. Moreover, we** 21 **show that non-genetic substitutions may provide a distinct route for exploring protein** 22 **sequence space, circumventing the mutational constraints imposed by the genetic code.** 23 **In addition, we provide experimental validation of non-genetic substitution on selected** 24 **purified proteins. We demonstrate specific and recurring non-genetic variation patterns** 25 **upon amino acid starvation in proteome-wide analyses of cancer-derived cell lines and** 26 **identify hundreds of substituted non-genetic proteoforms that recur consistently in** 27 **multiple healthy individuals or map to annotated protein functional sites. We propose** 28 **that these substitutions constitute a novel class of functional protein phenotypic variants.** 29 **Collectively, our findings indicate that non-genetic amino acid substitutions in human** 30 **proteins provide an abundant source to expanding the functional proteome.** 31

34 Genomes provide blueprint for the majority of proteins. However, it has become clear that the 35 complexity of the human proteome extends beyond the canonical set of ~20,000 protein-coding 36 genes<sup>2</sup> . The molecular determinants of cellular phenotype arise from an interplay between 37 alternative splicing<sup>3</sup> , posttranslational modifications<sup>4</sup> , heterozygosicity<sup>5</sup> , somatic mutations<sup>6</sup> , 38 microproteins and “peptideins”<sup>7</sup> , and phenotypic variants generated by transcriptional or 39 translational errors<sup>8,9</sup> . Translation errors can diversify proteomes by through amino acid 40 substitutions<sup>9</sup> , ribosomal frame-shifting<sup>10</sup> and STOP codon readthrough<sup>11</sup> . These processes 41 may offer myriad ways to fine-tune cellular phenotypes. 42 Human heterozygosity also increases protein heterogeneity by expressing both maternal and 43 paternal alleles. These alternative proteins may differ subtly in structure, function, stability, or 44 solubility, resulting in various effects on cellular fitness<sup>12</sup> . Notably, allele-specific gene 45 regulation can further expand the proteome’s diversity<sup>13</sup> . For instance, cell differentiation or 46 metabolism genes may display differential allelic expression<sup>5</sup> . Heterozygosity can enhance 47 resilience against pathogenic stressors<sup>14</sup> , mitigate the impact of deleterious homozygous 48 mutations<sup>15</sup> , or influence therapeutic responses<sup>16</sup> . 49 Somatic mutations, also add to the encoded proteomic diversity. Although somatic mutations 50 are frequently linked to senescence, and malignant growth, they can also provide selective 51 advantages<sup>17</sup> . The foremost example is error-prone DNA repair in B-cells, which deliberately 52 fosters diversity in immunoglobulin production<sup>18</sup> . Yet demonstration of the DNA variants at 53 the protein level of immunoglobulins, and their quantification is still limited<sup>19</sup> . Beyond 54 antibodies, other instances of beneficial somatic mutations have been reported, though they 55 remain relatively scarce and primarily confined to specific clinical contexts<sup>20</sup> . Still, as somatic 56 variation is omnipresent and pervasive, unraveling its broader role in human physiology and 57 adaptation represents a considerable challenge<sup>6</sup> . 58 In addition to genetically encoded proteoforms, protein variants resulting from errors in 59 transcription and/or translation (“phenotypic variants”) represent a large fraction of the “phenotypic variants”) represent a large fraction of the phenotypic variants”) represent a large fraction of the ”) represent a large fraction of the ) represent a large fraction of the 60 heterogeneous proteome. A prime characteristic 67 of phenotypic mutations is that they cast a significant burden on organisms. Proteins translated 68 with errors tend to misfold, aggregate, engage in spurious interactions, saturate the protein 69 quality control machinery<sup>25</sup> , and cause diseases<sup>26</sup> , e.g. neurodegeneration<sup>27</sup> . In parallel, an 70 increasing number of reports indicate that some errors in translation can be advantageous at the 71 cellular level<sup>25,28,29</sup> . In cancer, a recent summary provides evidence that translational errors 72 contribute to the tumor’s capacity to evolve<sup>30</sup> . On an evolutionary scale, phenotypic errors 73 might open adaptive paths otherwise precluded by epistatic interactions<sup>31</sup> , of purging of 74 deleterious mutations<sup>32</sup> , or expose hidden functionalities<sup>33</sup> . Whether deleterious or beneficial, 75 the rates and nature of phenotypic mutations appear regulated<sup>34</sup> and the tendency to make or 76 avoid them is postulated to be genetically encoded<sup>9,35</sup> . 77 **Results** 78 **Substitution search and validation pipeline** 79 80 We developed an improved approach towards detection of amino acid substitutions within 81 proteins, using mass spectrometric (MS) proteomic data. 204 Nevertheless, we experimentally assessed ionization efficiencies for seven 205 reference/substituted synthetic peptide pairs selected from cases in which the substituted 206 peptide exhibited higher MS1 intensity than its reference counterpart. In four out of seven pairs, 207 the substituted variants showed 10-100× higher ionization efficiency than the corresponding 208 reference peptides (Extended Data Fig. 4). However, the magnitude of these ionization 209 efficiency differences was insufficient to fully account for the observed disparities in MS1 210 intensities. We therefore propose that a combination of factors (including differential ionization 211 efficiency, noisy quantification at low signal levels, and chromatographic biases) may 212 overestimate the abundance of substituted (non-genetic) forms by up to 100–1,000-fold relative 213 to their reference variants. Accordingly, while the apparent abundance of substituted variants 214 may be inflated by technical factors, their true levels are likely more modest. Importantly, they 215 could still reach biologically meaningful abundances (on the order of single-digit percentages 216 relative to the reference form) consistent with our ability to confidently detect and validate such 217 variants even in low-abundance proteins. 218 **Expression ratios of genetically encoded protein variants** 219 **recapitulate their human population frequency** 220 221 We analyzed the abundance ratios of genetic SAAVs (heterozygous and somatic variants) 222 considering their allele frequencies (AF) in the human population from the gnomAD 4.1 223 database<sup>39</sup> (Supplementary Table 5). To classify identified substituent as heterozygotic allelic 224 variant, we required its log10 mRNA coverage ratio to be between –0.33 and 0.33 (maximum 225 ~2-fold transcript abundance difference) and minimal sequencing coverage of 10 reads. In total 226 630 unique variants fit into these criteria, for 498 of them AF annotations are available in the 227 gnomAD database. Most of these allelic variants expectedly show about equal protein 228 abundances of reference and substituted variant (Fig. 2). Nonetheless, some variants showed 229 markedly different protein abundance ratios than would be expected from their mRNA 230 expression ratios. Remarkably, annotated rare variants in human population also tend to have 231 lower abundance in comparison to the co-expressed reference variants corresponding to the 232 more frequent allele variant. Despite potential confounding effect in differential ionization 233 efficiency of SAAV peptides, we observed a positive correlation between the variant’s human

Our data suggest that the 249 frequencies of _intra-_ individual _de novo_ somatic mutations recapitulate the _inter-_ individual 250 population AFs established by organismal selection. Pvalues in (d-f) were obtained by Pearson correlation significance 275 test. 276 **Non-genetic variants likely consist of mistranslations and show** 277 **ribosomal error patterns** 278 279 Variants without RNA-sequencing support for the substituted sequence (6,510 substitutions 280 with reference residue coverage  10, of which 3,561with the coverage  100 reads) represent 281 the substantial part of the reported SAAVs. We assume that most of these substitutions consist 282 of frequently occurring translation errors.<sup>9,22,25</sup> . 283 Notably, the abundant substitutions observed in our and other analyses - I>V<sup>41</sup> , Y>F<sup>42</sup> and 284 S>N<sup>43</sup> reflect high levels of mistranslation within specific substituted positions of proteins 285 rather than a uniform trend across the proteome. Consequently, particular substitutions appear 286 to be more prevalent in some protein contexts than in others, indicating a potential underlying 287 mechanism involving either _cis_ or _trans_ regulation of translation errors. Our analysis revealed 288 an unexpectedly high prevalence of C>A, C>S, H>D, M>D, and W>D substitutions across the 289 dataset (Fig. 4b). These classes of substitutions were abundant among identifications from all 290 three substitution detection pipelines tested here (Supplementary Tables 1, 2, and 3). Literature 291 review suggests that these events can arise from technical chemical transformations: C>A/S 292 has been associated with desulfurization during proteomic sample preparation<sup>44</sup> ; H>D has been 293 reported following sample oxidation<sup>45</sup> ; and M>D and W>D has been observed under specific 294 conditions such as harsh transition metal-catalyzed oxidation<sup>46,47</sup> . Thus, we consider this class 295 of substitutions to potentially comprise a mixture of non-biological and biological events, as 296 we consistently detect them in additional datasets that were not exposed to overt oxidative 297 damage or desulfurization-promoting reagents (see further below). Accordingly, we flag these 298 substitutions as cautionary in the main text (Fig. 4b) and supplementary data and treat them as 299 non-biological unless supported by orthogonal evidence. All analyses of non-genetic variation 300 from healthy tissue data presented here exclude these five substitution types (5,216 variants 301 without RNA-seq support), unless stated otherwise.

Origin totals combine opportunity 313 in the detectable proteome with error propensity, while destination totals highlight recurrent 314 mistranslation products (Supplementary Table 6). 315 To assess the functional relevance of non-genetic substitutions in the biological context we 316 investigated four additional MS datasets of human cancer-derived cells cultured under 317 tryptophan, tyrosine, leucine, or arginine depletion<sup>52–54</sup> . We identified both previously reported 318 and novel substitutions under these conditions. We confirmed reported increase in W>F and 319 Y>F under tryptophan and tyrosine depletion, respectively (Fig. 4c, left)<sup>52</sup> . We also 320 corroborated the reported increase in R>K, R>C, R>H, and R>S substitutions under arginine 321 depletion, extending the original analysis to a proteome-wide scale (Fig. 4c, top right). Notably, 322 leucine depletion led more frequently to L>F and L>V (Fig. 4c, bottom right) in comparison 323 to negative control. Additionally, leucine starvation also induced a prominent M>T substitution 324 that was not detected in any non-starved control replicates (Fig. 4c, bottom right). We performed a separate functional analysis on non377 genetic and genetic substitutions in our dataset. To classify non-genetic substitution, we 378 specified a minimum RNA sequencing coverage threshold as 10 reads per reference and 0 reads 379 per substituted position. We observed a negative correlation between predicted pathogenicity 380 and the substitution abundance ratio in both genetic and non-genetic variant groups, indicating 381 that more disruptive substitutions tend to be present at lower levels in the proteome (Fig. 5a). 382 For genetic variants, this relationship likely reflects the greater disruptive potential of low383 abundance somatic substitutions relative to germline variants. The analogous trend among non384 genetic variants is consistent with either (i) preferential synthesis of non-pathogenic variants 385 or, more plausibly, (ii) enhanced degradation of more deleterious protein variants. Notably, 386 correlation with predicted pathogenicity is weak and cannot fully explain observed abundance 387 ratios. Moreover, non-genetic substitutions classified as pathogenic cannot impose a 388 comparable fitness burden, as they are incorporated into a fraction of a protein’s molecules 389 rather than uniformly affecting all copies, as implicitly assumed by AlphaMissense. Such 390 partial incorporation could expand functional diversity while avoiding the full fitness cost of a 391 fixed genetic mutation. 392 **Figure 5. For each observed substitution, we computed its linear 644 distance (number of residues between the sites along the protein sequence) to the nearest 645 annotated functional site and summarized these distances by the median across substitutions. 646 We then compared the observed median distances to a null distribution generated from 20,000 647 simulated datasets in which substitution positions were randomized within the MS-observed 648 regions of the corresponding protein sequences. 649 **GnomAD analysis** 650 Each MS-observed amino acid was assigned a reference genome codon extracted from the CDS 651 file associate with v112 ensembl genome release. Genomic coordinates for each codon 652 corresponding to the MS-observed substitution were extracted with ensembldb utility in R<sup>75</sup> . 653 The table containing genomic coordinates for the MS-observed substitutions was joined with 654 GnomAD v 4.1 exome data downloaded at <u>https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/</u> containing 655 collection of SNPs, their genomic location and their corresponding population allele 656 frequencies<sup>39</sup> . This joined table was filtered only for such SNPs which would result in MS657 observed missense substitution using custom python script. The substitution abundances were 658 evaluated considering their hypothetical allele frequencies within the human population. Three 659 groups of substitutions were evaluated – heterozygotic alleles, somatic variants and variants – heterozygotic alleles, somatic variants and variants  heterozygotic alleles, somatic variants and variants 660 without RNA support. All variants with sequencing support were filtered towards elimination 661

667 **Immunoglobulin analysis** 668 The sequences of proteins with MS-observed substitutions and which associated with GO terms 669 “immunoglobulin complex” and “antigen binding” (GO codes) were analyzed by the IgBlast 670 tool<sup>76</sup> . Blastp program was used with KABAT as variable domain delineation system<sup>77</sup> . The 671 tabular output was parsed by custom python script to extract the variable domain regions from 672 the alignment (CDR’s and FR’s). Substitutions with and without genetic support were analyzed 673 for their location within or outside the immunoglobulin annotated region. 674 **Calculation of amino acid substitution fractions** 675 Amino acid counts from the unique peptides yielded from reference proteome search (first 676 search of the pipeline) for all the analyzed tissues were aggregated together. Next all unique 677 amino acid substitutions originating from each kind of amino acid throughout all the samples 678 were also counted. Substitutions fraction for a given pair of origin and destination amino acid 679 was calculated as a fraction of observed substituted origin amino acids to the total number of 680 observed amino acids of this kind. 681 **Synthetic peptide analysis** 682 All synthetic peptides were ordered from GenScript (>=98% purity). The sample was then further diluted to 50 685 fmol/ul, and 9 ul were injected into the instrument. The resulting peptides were analyzed using 686 nanoflow liquid chromatography (nanoAcquity) coupled to high-resolution, high mass 687 accuracy mass spectrometry (Fusion Lumos). Data was searched against the list of peptides 688 using the Byonic search engine and quantified using Skyline. 689 **Proteomic sample preparation** 690 Pure proteins (GAPDH (MedChemExpress, HY-P78776), PRDX6 (CusaBio, CSB691 MP018659HU), PARK7 (HUABio, HUA-HA211158) and Hemoglobin (MP-Bio, MPB692 0855914)) were dissolved from lyophilized powder with 5% SDS in 50 mM Tris-HCl. 30ug 693 was used for digestion

Organs (Fig 1A) - _https://_ 741 _BioRender.com/5l6nzom; ribosome (Fig 1C) -_ _<u>https://BioRender.com/6ozp6rp; mRNA (Fig 1A) -</u>_ 742 _<u>https://BioRender.com/wzjcs3i</u>_ ; mRNA (Fig 1C)  - _<u>https://BioRender.com/88yiadq</u>_ <u>; antibody (Fig 1C</u> 743 and Fig 2) - _https://BioRender.com/ mhmqdpo_ 744 745 **Conclusion** 746 747 In conclusion, our data reveal that unity and multiplicity coexist within the proteome: the 748 genome’s unique signature is represented not just by a single encoded form, but rather by a 749 spectrum of functionally relevant proteoforms that blur the line between individual and 750 population. Our study, therefore, provides a unique perspective on an additional layer of 751 genetic design complexity, highlighting the existence of a functional, recurrent, and evolvable 752 protein quasi-species within the human proteome.

#### <u>Reporting Summary</u> 

Nature Portfolio wishes to improve the reproducibility of the work that we publish. This form provides structure for consistency and transparency in reporting. For further information on Nature Portfolio policies, see our <u>Editorial Policies</u> and the <u>Editorial Policy Checklist.</u> 

###### <u>Statistics</u> 

For all statistical analyses, confirm that the following items are present in the figure legend, table legend, main text, or Methods section. 

###### n/a Confirmed 

The exact sample size ( _n_ ) for each experimental group/condition, given as a discrete number and unit of measurement 

A statement on whether measurements were taken from distinct samples or whether the same sample was measured repeatedly 

The statistical test(s) used AND whether they are one- or two-sided 

_Only common tests should be described solely by name; describe more complex techniques in the Methods section._ 

- A description of all covariates tested 

A description of any assumptions or corrections, such as tests of normality and adjustment for multiple comparisons 

A full description of the statistical parameters including central tendency (e.g. means) or other basic estimates (e.g. regression coefficient) AND variation (e.g. standard deviation) or associated estimates of uncertainty (e.g. confidence intervals) 

For null hypothesis testing, the test statistic (e.g. _F_ , _t_ , _r_ ) with confidence intervals, effect sizes, degrees of freedom and _P_ value noted _Give P values as exact values whenever suitable._ 

For Bayesian analysis, information on the choice of priors and Markov chain Monte Carlo settings 

For hierarchical and complex designs, identification of the appropriate level for tests and full reporting of outcomes 

Estimates of effect sizes (e.g. Cohen's _d_ , Pearson's _r_ ), indicating how they were calculated 

_Our web collection on_ _<u>statistics for biologists contains articles on many of the points above.</u>_

##### Life <u>sciences study design</u> 

All studies must disclose on these points even when the disclosure is negative. 

Sample size For public data, we analyzed all available samples for each described experiment in this manuscript to obtain the most data. For experimental samples we ran one measurement per purified protein as the purpose of the analysis was to qualitatively confirm substitution existence without ambition to maximize the detections of all substitutions 

Data exclusions PXD010154 healthy tissue data - 27/29 tissues were analyzed; kidney and liver samples were not accompanied with clear RNAseq data PXD027328  degradomics dataset - non fractionated samples were excluded due to low proteomic depth PXD017276  in vitro differentiated RBC precursors - all RBC samples were analyzed PXD043612  arginine starvation dataset - all fractionated samples were analyzed PXD044085  leucine starvation dataset - all fractionated samples were analyzed PXD028921  tryptophan/phenylalanine starvation dataset - all fractionated samples were analyzed 

2 

Replication All experiments were performed in one replicate as the purpose of the analysis was to demonstrate the existence of substituted species and eventually to validate specific substitution types also identified in public data. No quantitative claims were raised. Confirmation of specific substitutions was performed using combination of our experimental datasets and publicly available data Randomization We did not perform randomization in our experiments as our purified protein samples had no comparison groups. Blinding We did not perform blinding as we focused on aggregated analysis of substitutions in humans without discrimination into groups
